title: Sum of Total Strength of Wizards
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every subarray directly versus the monotonic stack contribution technique extended with a prefix-of-prefix-sums layer.

sections.title: Sum of Total Strength of Wizards

content.title: Sum of Total Strength of Wizards

blocks.text: You are given a 0-indexed integer array strength, where strength[i] denotes the strength of the i-th wizard. For a contiguous subarray, its TOTAL STRENGTH is the product of two values: the strength of the WEAKEST wizard in it, and the SUM of all strengths in it. Return the sum of the total strengths of EVERY contiguous subarray, modulo 10^9 + 7.

blocks.caption: The monotonic stack "contribution technique" finds each element's minimum-boundaries; a prefix-sum-of-prefix-sums trick then totals every affected subarray's own sum in O(1)

blocks.text: This directly builds on Sum of Subarray Minimums: instead of just counting how many subarrays each element is the minimum of, this problem needs the SUM of THOSE SPECIFIC subarrays' own sums, multiplied by the minimum value, then totaled across every element.

blocks.title: Analogy: Weighing In Not Just Who's Weakest, But the Whole Team's Combined Weight Too
blocks.text: Building on the earlier "who is the weakest member of every possible team" idea, this problem additionally asks: for every team where a specific person IS the weakest, what is the SUM of that entire team's combined weight, and how does that interact with who is weakest? Rather than just counting how many teams a person is weakest in, the actual combined weights of ALL of those specific teams must be totaled up too, requiring a cleverer running-total trick (summing sums, not just counting).

blocks.caption: For each element, the same left/right boundary counts from the minimum-contribution technique bound WHICH subarrays to sum; a second prefix-of-prefix layer totals those subarray sums directly

blocks.text: Before computing each subarray's (min * sum) individually via an O(n^2) or worse approach, recognize this as an extension of the monotonic stack contribution technique: for each element as the minimum, the SAME left/right boundaries used in Sum of Subarray Minimums determine WHICH subarrays to consider; the new challenge is efficiently summing THEIR sums, requiring an additional layer of prefix sums.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Just like Sum of Subarray Minimums, each element strength[i] contributes strength[i] multiplied by something, across every subarray where it is the minimum, bounded by prevLess[i] (strictly smaller, left) and nextLessOrEqual[i] (right).

Observation 2: Unlike that simpler problem (which only needed a COUNT of such subarrays), here that "something" must be the SUM of every one of those specific subarrays' own sums, since the total strength also depends on the sum, not just the count.

Observation 3: The sum of a subarray [s, e] can be written as prefix[e+1] - prefix[s], using a standard prefix sum array. Summing this over all valid (s, e) pairs (s ranging over left choices, e ranging over right choices) can be REARRANGED into two separate sums: a sum of prefix[e+1] terms (weighted by how many left choices exist) minus a sum of prefix[s] terms (weighted by how many right choices exist).

Observation 4: Both of those rearranged sums are themselves just RANGES of the prefix array, summable in O(1) using a SECOND prefix sum array (a prefix sum OF the prefix sums), avoiding ever looping over individual (s, e) pairs.

This extends the monotonic stack contribution technique with an additional layer of prefix sums: the same boundary-finding logic determines WHICH subarrays matter, while prefix-sum-of-prefix-sums totals their individual sums directly, all in O(n) overall.
Directly enumerate every subarray, tracking its running minimum and running sum as it extends, and accumulate min * sum for each one.

items: For each starting index i, extend the subarray one element at a time, tracking the running minimum and running sum.
At each extension, compute min * sum for that specific subarray and add it (mod 10^9+7) to a running total.

codes.python:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def total_strength(strength):
    n = len(strength)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        min_val = strength[i]
        running_sum = 0
        for j in range(i, n):                                              # extend the subarray one element at a time
            min_val = min(min_val, strength[j])
            running_sum += strength[j]
            total = (total + min_val * running_sum) % MOD
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(total_strength([1, 3, 1, 2]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking BOTH the running minimum and running sum incrementally avoids rescanning the entire subarray at every extension.
This directly implements the problem's definition, but at O(n^2) total work, since every subarray is individually processed.

blocks.text: Correctly computes the exact total, since every subarray's min and sum are directly and correctly tracked.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2), enumerating all O(n^2) subarrays.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^2) does not scale to the problem's constraints (up to 10^5 elements); the monotonic stack contribution technique, extended with a second prefix-sum layer, achieves O(n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force processes each subarray individually. Instead, reuse the exact monotonic stack boundaries (prevLess, nextLessOrEqual) from Sum of Subarray Minimums to determine, for each element, WHICH subarrays it is the minimum of. Then, instead of just counting them, use a prefix-sum-of-prefix-sums array to directly total the SUM of all of those specific subarrays' own sums in O(1), by algebraically splitting the double sum into two independently-summable ranges.

Build prefix[k] (sum of the first k elements) and prefixOfPrefix[k] (sum of prefix[0..k-1]). Compute left[i] (previous strictly smaller index) and right[i] (next smaller-or-equal index) via two monotonic stack passes. For each i: leftCount = i - left[i], rightCount = right[i] - i; sumOfEndTerms = prefixOfPrefix[right[i]+1] - prefixOfPrefix[i+1]; sumOfStartTerms = prefixOfPrefix[i+1] - prefixOfPrefix[left[i]+1]; combined = leftCount * sumOfEndTerms - rightCount * sumOfStartTerms; add strength[i] * combined (mod 10^9+7) to the answer.
Reuse the monotonic stack boundaries from the minimum-contribution technique, and use a prefix-sum-of-prefix-sums layer to total each affected subarray's sum in O(1) per element.
Verified correctness for strength = [1,3,1,2] and strength = [5,4,6]

blocks.title: Why this cross-verification matters
blocks.text: Because this derivation involves subtracting two large prefix-of-prefix sums (each individually reduced modulo 10^9+7), confirming the optimized formula against the straightforward brute force on real examples is the most reliable way to catch a sign or off-by-one error in the algebraic rearrangement before trusting it.

codes.python:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def total_strength(strength):
    n = len(strength)
    prefix = [0] * (n + 1)                                                  # prefix[k] = sum of strength[0..k-1]
    for i in range(n):
        prefix[i + 1] = (prefix[i] + strength[i]) % MOD

    prefix_of_prefix = [0] * (n + 2)                                        # prefix_of_prefix[k] = sum of prefix[0..k-1]
    for i in range(n + 1):
        prefix_of_prefix[i + 1] = (prefix_of_prefix[i] + prefix[i]) % MOD

    left = [-1] * n                                                         # nearest index to the left with a STRICTLY smaller value
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and strength[stack[-1]] >= strength[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)

    right = [n] * n                                                         # nearest index to the right with a value <= strength[i]
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and strength[i] < strength[stack[-1]]:
            stack.pop()
        right[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n
        stack.append(i)

    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        l, r = left[i], right[i]
        left_count = i - l                                                 # number of valid LEFT edges for subarrays where i is the min
        right_count = r - i                                                # number of valid RIGHT edges
        # sum over every such subarray's OWN sum, using prefix-of-prefix to total it in O(1)
        sum_of_end_terms = (prefix_of_prefix[r + 1] - prefix_of_prefix[i + 1]) % MOD
        sum_of_start_terms = (prefix_of_prefix[i + 1] - prefix_of_prefix[l + 1]) % MOD
        combined = (left_count * sum_of_end_terms - right_count * sum_of_start_terms) % MOD
        total = (total + strength[i] * combined) % MOD
    return total % MOD


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(total_strength([1, 3, 1, 2]))
    print(total_strength([5, 4, 6]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): two monotonic stack passes, two prefix-sum passes, and one final O(n) combination pass.
Space: O(n), for the prefix arrays, boundary arrays, and stacks.

The sum of a subarray [s, e] is prefix[e+1] - prefix[s]. Summing this over EVERY valid (s, e) pair (s from left+1 to i, e from i to right-1) splits into two independent sums by linearity: a sum of prefix[e+1] terms, each counted once per valid LEFT choice (hence multiplied by leftCount), minus a sum of prefix[s] terms, each counted once per valid RIGHT choice (hence multiplied by rightCount). Both of THOSE sums are themselves just contiguous RANGES within the prefix array, directly computable via ANOTHER prefix-sum array (prefixOfPrefix) in O(1), avoiding ever looping over individual (s, e) pairs.

items: prefix and prefixOfPrefix are each simple, standard prefix-sum arrays, just applied one layer deeper than usual.
The modulo arithmetic requires an extra "+ MOD" before the final "% MOD" on subtractions, since intermediate differences can otherwise go negative.
left[i] and right[i] are computed via the EXACT SAME two monotonic stack passes as Sum of Subarray Minimums, directly reusing that already-understood technique.

blocks.text: When a "sum over subarrays" problem needs not just a COUNT of qualifying subarrays but the SUM of their own sums, a second layer of prefix sums (prefix sums OF prefix sums) extends the standard monotonic stack contribution technique to compute that total in O(1) per element, via an algebraic splitting of the double sum.

items: Forgetting the extra "+ MOD" before the final modulo on subtractions, risking a negative intermediate result under modular arithmetic.
Reusing the SAME tie-breaking rule on both boundary searches (instead of strict-left, non-strict-right), which would double-count subarrays with duplicate minimum values.
Attempting to compute the sum-of-sums with a single prefix-sum layer, missing that a genuinely SECOND layer (prefix of prefix) is required for this specific double-summation.

items: Explicitly stating "this is Sum of Subarray Minimums, but needing SUM instead of COUNT, requiring one more layer of prefix sums" demonstrates recognizing this as a direct, well-motivated extension of a known technique, rather than an entirely new problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "min * sum over ALL subarrays" points toward the monotonic stack contribution technique (for finding min-boundaries) COMBINED WITH a second layer of prefix sums (for totaling subarray sums directly).

items: How does this problem build directly on Sum of Subarray Minimums? It reuses the EXACT SAME left/right boundary-finding logic; the only difference is replacing a simple count multiplication with a prefix-of-prefix-sum-based total.

Why is a SECOND layer of prefix sums specifically needed here, and not just one? Because the quantity being summed (a subarray's sum) is ITSELF already a difference of prefix sums; summing THAT over a range requires prefix sums of the prefix sum array itself.

How would you extend this to also handle the MAXIMUM (not just minimum) as one factor? The identical technique applies, using the max-boundary monotonic stack passes (as in Sum of Subarray Ranges) instead of the min-boundary ones.

A significant extension of the monotonic stack contribution technique from Sum of Subarray Minimums elsewhere in this category, adding a second prefix-sum layer to handle summing subarray sums rather than merely counting subarrays.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic stack + prefix-of-prefix sums): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic stack contribution technique, extended with a second layer of prefix sums

Core Idea: The same min-boundaries from Sum of Subarray Minimums determine which subarrays matter; a prefix-sum-of-prefix-sums array totals THEIR sums directly in O(1), via an algebraic split of the double sum
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Summing a RANGE of subarray sums requires a SECOND prefix-sum layer, since each individual subarray sum is already itself a difference of first-layer prefix sums
Interview Difficulty: Hard
